        extensions: [".md", ".txt", ".csv", ".py", ".json", ".html"]
        recursive: true

agents:
  - id: main
    brain:
      provider: deepseek
      backend: openai_compat
      model: deepseek-chat
      config:
        api_key: "{{env.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}}"
        base_url: "https://api.deepseek.com/v1"
      temperature: 0.0
      max_tokens: 2048
    system_prompt: |
      Tu es un assistant qui répond aux questions en utilisant UNIQUEMENT
      les documents de ta knowledge base. Cherche d'abord avec rag.query,
      puis réponds avec des citations précises.
      Si l'info n'est pas dans les sources, dis "Non trouvé dans les documents."

execution:
  mode: one_shot
  input:
    type: text
  output:
    type: text

knowledge_base/examples/01-scheduled-mon.content:
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEMPLATE 01 — Scheduled Monitor (Job Hunter)
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Pattern: "Surveille X périodiquement"
# Use case: Hourly job-board scraper — every user pre-fills a CV +
#           preferences once, the daemon replays them into every cron
#           tick as if the user were typing live.
#
# What this template demonstrates:
#   • mode: background + cron trigger (hourly)
#   • payload_schema with required prompt + typed metadata + file slot
#   • multi-session (one independent payload per user)
#   • web.search + web.fetch for crawling
#   • memory for tracking already-seen jobs (no duplicates)
#   • filesystem.write for emitting a daily report
#
# Adapt this template by:
#   • changing the cron schedule
#   • renaming/adding metadata fields in payload_schema.metadata
#   • swapping web.search filters (allowed_domains/blocked_domains)
#   • plugging an outbound channel (telegram/email/slack) for delivery
#
# The agent NEVER reads the CV with filesystem.read — the daemon
# inlines it as a base64 document block at trigger time.
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app:
  app_id: scheduled-monitor
  name: "Scheduled Monitor (Job Hunter)"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "Hourly background agent that searches job boards using your CV and preferences."
  icon: "🎯"
  color: "#FF6B6B"
  category: "productivity"
  author: "Digitorn"
  tags: [background, cron, web, payload, multi-user]

modules:
  web:
    config:
      search:
        primary: duckduckgo
  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true
      todo_list: false
  filesystem: {}

agents:
  - id: hunter
    role: worker
    brain:
      # Default to Claude Code OAuth — works on any dev machine that
      # has `claude` authenticated. To use a real API key in
      # production, swap to: api_key: "{{env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}}"
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 4096
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 6
    system_prompt: |
      You are a personal job-hunting agent.

      Every hour the user does NOT type anything — the daemon hands you
      the user's pre-filled prompt, structured preferences, and CV
      directly in the user message. Treat that input exactly as if the
      user had just typed it in a chat.

      ## Your job each tick
      1. Read the user's prompt + preferences carefully.
      2. The CV is already attached (PDF document block) — extract the
         relevant skills/experience. NEVER call filesystem.read on it.
      3. Use web.search to find new job postings matching the profile.
         Be specific: combine prompt keywords with metadata.location and
         metadata.contract_type.
      4. For each promising hit, web.fetch the listing page and extract:
            - title, company, location, salary range
            - 3-line summary of the role
            - a match score 0–100 against the CV
      5. Skip postings you've already seen (use memory.recall to check).
         Persist new postings via memory.remember so you don't repeat
         them on the next tick.
      6. Write a short markdown report to
         `~/jobhunt-reports/{{ '{{' }}now.iso{{ '}}' }}.md` with the top 5 matches.
      7. End your turn with a one-paragraph summary of what you found.

      ## Quality bar
      - Only surface jobs that actually match the CV. A bad match is
        worse than no match at all — the user is busy.
      - Salary range is a hard filter: skip anything below
        metadata.min_salary.
      - If `metadata.remote_only` is true, skip on-site listings.

      ## Boundaries
      - Never apply on the user's behalf — only report.
      - Never store personal data outside the report file.
      - Stop after 8 tool calls maximum to keep cost predictable.

execution:
  mode: background
  entry_agent: hunter
  max_turns: 8
  timeout: 180

  session_mode: multi
  max_sessions_per_user: 5
  max_concurrent_activations: 10

  triggers:
    - id: hourly-search
      type: cron
      schedule: "0 * * * *"
      routing: broadcast
      message: "Time for the hourly job search."

  payload_schema:
    required: true

    prompt:
      required: true
      label: "What kind of role are you looking for?"
      placeholder: "Senior Python engineer, remote, ML or data infrastructure focus"
      description: "Be specific — the agent reuses this prompt every hour."
      min_length: 20
      max_length: 1000

    metadata:
      - name: location
        label: "Preferred city / region"
        type: string
        required: true
        placeholder: "Berlin, Lisbon, anywhere in EU"
      - name: min_salary
        label: "Minimum yearly salary (€)"
        type: integer
        required: true
        default: 60000
        min: 0
        max: 500000
      - name: remote_only
        label: "Remote only?"
        type: boolean
        default: true
      - name: contract_type
        label: "Contract type"
        type: select
        options: [full_time, part_time, contract, freelance]
        default: full_time
      - name: notes
        label: "Anything else the agent should know?"
        type: text
        required: false
        placeholder: "Avoid crypto companies. Open to startups <50 people."

    files:
      - name: cv
        label: "Your CV"
        description: "PDF only, 5 MB max. Used by the agent on every tick."
        required: true
        mime: [application/pdf]
        max_size_mb: 5
        max_count: 1
      - name: portfolio
        label: "Portfolio / writing samples (optional)"
        description: "Up to 5 files. PDFs and images supported."
        required: false
        mime: [application/pdf, image/png, image/jpeg]
        max_size_mb: 10
        max_count: 5

capabilities:
  default_policy: auto
  max_risk_level: medium
  grant:
    - module: web
      actions: [search, fetch, extract]
    - module: memory
      actions: [remember, recall, forget, set_goal]
    - module: filesystem
      actions: [read, write, glob]

knowledge_base/examples/02-conversationa.content:
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEMPLATE 02 — Conversational Assistant (Telegram Support Bot)
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Pattern: "Bot conversationnel persistant"
# Use case: Customer-support / personal-assistant Telegram bot. Each
#           Telegram chat becomes its own session with its own memory,
#           workspace, and (optional) per-user preferences.
#
# What this template demonstrates:
#   • mode: background WITHOUT a cron trigger — the channel IS the trigger
#   • channels.providers.telegram_bot — bidirectional adapter
#   • activation block: render the user's message + auto-reply
#   • session_mode: mono — 1 session per chat_id, auto-created on first DM
#   • payload_schema OPTIONAL — preferences (tone, language) only,
#     no required prompt. The chat itself is the "input".
#   • memory module configured for persistent per-session recall
#
# Adapt this template by:
#   • swapping telegram for slack/discord/email (same channels module
#     with a different `adapter:` value)
#   • tightening allowed_chat_ids for a private bot
#   • changing the session template to group multiple chats together
#   • plugging additional outbound channels for cross-platform replies
#
# Conversational triggers do NOT need a payload_schema with a required
# prompt — the user types live every message. The schema here is purely
# for *persistent preferences* the agent should remember about each user.
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app:
  app_id: conversational-assistant
  name: "Conversational Assistant (Telegram)"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "Persistent Telegram support bot — each chat has its own memory and preferences."
  icon: "💬"
  color: "#0088CC"
  category: "assistant"
  author: "Digitorn"
  tags: [background, channels, telegram, conversational, multi-user]

modules:
  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true
      todo_list: false
      runtime:
        goal_guardian: false

  web:
    config:
      search:
        primary: duckduckgo

  channels:
    config:
      default_agent: assistant
      max_turns: 10
      timeout: 60
      providers:
        telegram_bot:
          adapter: telegram
          config:
            # Stored in the per-app secret store, not in the YAML.
            # Set with: digitorn secrets set conversational-assistant TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN <token>
            token: "{{secret.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}}"
            poll_timeout: 30
            # Uncomment to restrict the bot to a whitelist of chats:
            # allowed_chat_ids: [123456789, 987654321]
          activation:
            # The user's message becomes the agent's user_message.
            message: "{{event.payload.text}}"
            # Extra system context appended to the agent's system prompt.
            context: |
              Telegram user: {{event.payload.display_name}} (chat {{event.payload.chat_id}})
              Chat type: {{event.payload.chat_type}}
            # Auto-reply: the agent's final response is sent back to the
            # same Telegram chat. No need to call any send_message tool.
            reply: auto
            # Per-chat persistent session — memory and history are
            # preserved across messages for this chat_id.
            session: "tg-{{event.payload.chat_id}}"

agents:
  - id: assistant
    role: worker
    brain:
      # OAuth fallback — works on any dev machine with `claude` installed.
      # In production swap to: api_key: "{{env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}}"
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.4
      max_tokens: 2048
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 8
        auto_compact: true
    system_prompt: |
      You are a helpful, concise personal assistant on Telegram.

      ## Context
      - Each conversation is one Telegram chat.
      - You have persistent memory across messages — use memory.recall
        at the start of every conversation to retrieve what you know
        about this user, and memory.remember to store useful new facts.
      - The user's pre-set preferences (tone, language) are injected at
        the top of every system prompt — honour them strictly.

      ## Style
      - Keep replies short. Telegram users expect 1-3 sentence answers,
        not essays. If a long answer is truly needed, break it into
        bullet points.
      - Match the user's language. If the user writes in French, reply
        in French. Same for any other language.
      - Be direct. Skip "Sure!", "Of course!", "I'd be happy to help".

      ## What you can do
      - Answer general questions (use web.search if you need fresh info).
      - Remember things the user tells you (memory.remember).
      - Recall past context (memory.recall).
      - Refuse anything outside your role — politely but clearly.

      ## What you must not do
      - Never make up facts. If you don't know, say so.
      - Never store sensitive data (passwords, credit cards, IDs) in
        memory — politely refuse if the user tries.
      - Never reply to messages that aren't addressed to you (e.g.
        random group-chat noise).

execution:
  mode: background
  entry_agent: assistant
  max_turns: 10
  timeout: 60

  # Mono session: one persistent session per Telegram chat. The session
  # is auto-created when the first message arrives — no API call needed.
  session_mode: mono
  max_concurrent_activations: 20

  # No triggers block — the channel adapter IS the trigger. Inbound
  # Telegram messages flow through the activation pipeline defined in
  # modules.channels.config.providers.telegram_bot.activation above.

  # Optional preferences. Conversational bots don't need a required
  # prompt (the user types live every message), but you can still expose
  # *persistent* settings the agent should respect on every reply.
  payload_schema:
    required: false   # bot works fine without preferences

    prompt:
      required: false
      label: "Persistent system instructions (optional)"
      placeholder: "Always reply in Spanish. Be very formal."
      description: "Anything here is injected into every reply for this user."
      max_length: 500

    metadata:
      - name: language
        label: "Preferred reply language"
        type: select
        options: [auto, en, fr, es, de, pt, it]
        default: auto
      - name: tone
        label: "Tone"
        type: select
        options: [neutral, friendly, formal, playful]
        default: neutral
      - name: emoji
        label: "Use emojis in replies?"
        type: boolean
        default: false
      - name: max_length
        label: "Maximum reply length (chars)"
        type: integer
        default: 500
        min: 50
        max: 4000

    files: []

capabilities:
  default_policy: auto
  max_risk_level: medium
  grant:
    - module: memory
      actions: [remember, recall, forget, set_goal]
    - module: web
      actions: [search, fetch]

knowledge_base/examples/03-event-webhook.content:
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEMPLATE 03 — Event Webhook Processor (GitHub PR Reviewer)
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Pattern: "Réagit à des événements externes"
# Use case: GitHub sends a webhook when a pull request is opened or
#           updated. The app validates the HMAC signature, persists the
#           PR metadata in a local SQLite DB, then spawns a sub-agent
#           to actually review the diff. The coordinator returns
#           immediately so GitHub doesn't time out.
#
# What this template demonstrates:
#   • channels.providers.github_pr — webhook adapter with HMAC auth
#   • activation.session — one durable session per PR (so updates to
#     the same PR continue the same review thread)
#   • activation.prepare — pre-fetch state from the DB before invoking
#     the agent (avoids replaying duplicate webhooks)
#   • database module — SQLite, zero-setup, persists PR reviews
#   • agent_spawn module — coordinator delegates the actual review to
#     a specialised sub-agent, fire-and-forget
#   • event-driven background mode (no cron, no payload schema — every
#     activation carries its own data in event.payload)
#
# Adapt this template by:
#   • swapping the github_pr provider for stripe / linear / shopify /
#     any other webhook source (signature_header changes per provider)
#   • plugging an outbound channel (slack/email) into the reviewer
#     sub-agent so it posts the review back to the team
#   • switching SQLite for postgres in modules.database.setup
#
# Deployment notes:
#   1. Set the secret: digitorn secrets set <app> WEBHOOK_SECRET <hmac>
#   2. Configure the GitHub webhook to POST to your-daemon/hook/github-pr
#   3. Set "Content type: application/json" + "Secret: <same WEBHOOK_SECRET>"
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app:
  app_id: event-webhook-processor
  name: "Event Webhook Processor (GitHub PR Reviewer)"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "Reviews GitHub pull requests via webhook with persistent history."
  icon: "🪝"
  color: "#24292F"
  category: "developer-tools"
  author: "Digitorn"
  tags: [background, channels, webhook, agent_spawn, database]

modules:
  # SQLite — zero-setup persistent store. Swap to postgres in production.
  database:
    setup:
      - action: connect
        params:
          connection_id: pr_db
          driver: sqlite
          url: "sqlite:///./.digitorn/pr-reviews.db"

  # Channels — the webhook IS the trigger.
  channels:
    config:
      default_agent: coordinator
      max_turns: 6
      timeout: 30
      providers:
        github_pr:
          adapter: webhook
          config:
            inbound_path: "/hook/github-pr"
            auth: signature
            signature_secret: "{{secret.WEBHOOK_SECRET}}"
            signature_header: "X-Hub-Signature-256"
            max_payload_bytes: 1048576  # 1 MB
          activation:
            # One durable session per PR — re-opens of the same PR
            # continue the same review thread instead of starting fresh.
            session: "pr-{{event.payload.pull_request.id}}"
            # The coordinator agent receives a clean summary of the PR.
            message: |
              GitHub PR event: {{event.payload.action}}
              PR #{{event.payload.pull_request.number}}: {{event.payload.pull_request.title}}
              Author: {{event.payload.pull_request.user.login}}
              Repository: {{event.payload.repository.full_name}}
              URL: {{event.payload.pull_request.html_url}}
              Changed files: {{event.payload.pull_request.changed_files}}
              Additions: {{event.payload.pull_request.additions}} / Deletions: {{event.payload.pull_request.deletions}}
            context: |
              You are processing an inbound GitHub webhook. The PR data
              is summarised in the user message above. Decide whether to
              spawn a reviewer sub-agent based on the action.
            # No auto-reply — webhooks are fire-and-forget. The reviewer
            # sub-agent will post back via a separate channel later.
            reply: none

  web:
    config:
      search:
        primary: duckduckgo

  filesystem: {}

  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true

agents:
  # ── Coordinator: triages every webhook, decides what to spawn ──
  - id: coordinator
    role: coordinator
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.1
      max_tokens: 1024
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 4
    plan_first: false
    system_prompt: |
      You are the triage coordinator for a GitHub PR review pipeline.

      ## Your job
      For each incoming webhook event you receive, you have ONE turn
      to decide what happens:

      1. If `action == "opened"` or `action == "synchronize"`:
         - Insert a row into the `reviews` table via database.sql
           (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS reviews(
              pr_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
              repo TEXT, title TEXT, status TEXT, created_at TEXT)).
         - spawn_agent("reviewer", task="Review PR #N in repo X",
           context={pr_url, pr_id, repo, title}).
         - Return immediately. DO NOT wait for the reviewer.

      2. If `action == "closed"` or `action == "merged"`:
         - Update the row's status in the reviews table.
         - Do not spawn anything.

      3. If `action == "edited"` or anything else:
         - Skip silently.

      ## Critical rules
      - You have at most 6 turns. Stay in 1-2.
      - NEVER write to the filesystem yourself — that's the reviewer's job.
      - NEVER call agent_wait. The reviewer is fire-and-forget.
      - Always end your turn with a single-line confirmation
        ("Triaged PR #N → reviewer spawned" or "Skipped non-actionable action X").

  # ── Reviewer: actually reads the diff and writes the review ──
  - id: reviewer
    role: specialist
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 4096
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 6
    system_prompt: |
      You are a senior code reviewer.

      ## Context
      You were spawned by the coordinator with a task like
      "Review PR #N in repo X". The PR's metadata (url, repo, title) is
      in your initial context block.

      ## Your job
      1. web.fetch the PR's `.diff` URL (append `.diff` to the html_url).
      2. Read the diff. Look for:
         - obvious bugs / null pointers / off-by-one
         - missing tests for new behaviour
         - security issues (injection, leaked secrets, missing auth)
         - architecture violations vs the rest of the repo
      3. Write a markdown review with these sections:
         - Summary (3 lines)
         - 🚨 Blocking issues
         - 🟡 Suggestions
         - ✅ What's good
      4. Save the review to
         `./.digitorn/pr-reviews/{{ '{{' }}now.iso{{ '}}' }}-pr-{N}.md`.
      5. Update the database row's status to "reviewed".

      ## Quality bar
      - Be specific. Quote the exact lines from the diff.
      - Be honest about uncertainty. If you don't fully understand the
        change, say so — don't bullshit.
      - Stop at 12 tool calls maximum.

execution:
  mode: background
  entry_agent: coordinator
  max_turns: 12
  timeout: 120

  # Mono = one durable session per PR (the channel routes by session
  # template above — pr-<id> — so every PR gets its own thread).
  session_mode: mono
  max_concurrent_activations: 30

  # No triggers block — the webhook adapter IS the trigger.

  # No payload_schema — webhook events carry all the data we need in
  # event.payload. There is nothing for the user to pre-fill.

capabilities:
  default_policy: auto
  max_risk_level: medium
  grant:
    - module: database
      actions: [connect, sql, schema]
    - module: agent_spawn
      actions: [agent]
    - module: web
      actions: [search, fetch, extract]
    - module: filesystem
      actions: [read, write, glob]
    - module: memory
      actions: [remember, recall]

knowledge_base/examples/04-document-pipe.content:
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEMPLATE 04 — Document Pipeline (Inbox Auto-Summarizer + RAG Indexer)
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Pattern: "Traite des fichiers en arrière-plan"
# Use case: Drop a PDF / Markdown / text file into ./inbox and the agent
#           reads it, writes a structured summary to ./summaries, and
#           ingests both the original and the summary into a local RAG
#           knowledge base so the user can later query "what was that
#           paper about transformers I read last month?".
#
# What this template demonstrates:
#   • channels.providers.inbox — file_watcher adapter (the modern way
#     to do file watching, replaces the legacy type: watch)
#   • activation.session: per_event — every dropped file is its own
#     fresh activation, no state bleed between files
#   • filesystem read/write/mkdir for the actual document handling
#   • lsp configured for ruff/eslint/etc — every file the agent writes
#     is auto-validated before the agent thinks it's done
#   • rag module — a local persistent knowledge base. The agent
#     ingests every processed file into the KB so it builds up over
#     time. Yes, RAG inside a template that goes inside the RAG that
#     powers the App Builder. It's RAG all the way down.
#   • NO payload schema — the dropped file IS the input, there is
#     nothing for the user to pre-fill
#
# Adapt this template by:
#   • changing the paths glob to watch a different folder / extensions
#   • swapping rag in-memory for a persistent qdrant path in production
#   • plugging an outbound channel (email/slack) to push the summary
#     somewhere when it's ready
#   • tightening the lsp linter list for your stack
#
# Operational notes:
#   - Files are processed at most once: the agent should refuse to
#     re-process a file whose path already exists in the rag KB.
#   - Failed activations don't move the file — the next poll cycle
#     will re-trigger them. Keep the agent idempotent.
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app:
  app_id: document-pipeline
  name: "Document Pipeline (Inbox Summarizer + RAG)"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "Watches an inbox folder, summarizes new files, and indexes them into a local RAG."
  icon: "📂"
  color: "#9B59B6"
  category: "productivity"
  author: "Digitorn"
  tags: [background, watch, filesystem, lsp, rag, document-processing]

modules:
  filesystem: {}

  # LSP — auto-runs on every filesystem.write() / filesystem.edit().
  # The agent doesn't have to call it explicitly: the result of the
  # write tool will already include lint diagnostics if the file is in
  # one of the configured languages.
  lsp:
    config:
      python: "ruff check --output-format=json --select=E,F,W,I,N,UP,B"
      # Add more languages by uncommenting:
      # typescript: "eslint --format json"
      # go: "golangci-lint run --out-format json"

  # Local RAG — persists at ./.digitorn/document-rag/.qdrant on disk.
  # The agent uses it as its long-term memory of every document it has
  # processed, so it can answer "what was in that report I uploaded
  # last week?" weeks later.
  rag:
    backend:
      type: qdrant
      path: "./.digitorn/document-rag"

  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true
      todo_list: false

  # File watcher channel — every file matching the paths glob fires a
  # fresh activation. The full file path is in event.payload.path.
  channels:
    config:
      default_agent: librarian
      max_turns: 10
      timeout: 120
      providers:
        inbox:
          adapter: file_watcher
          config:
            # Watch the inbox for new files. The agent writes summaries
            # to ./summaries — make sure that folder is OUTSIDE the
            # watched glob or you'll trigger a feedback loop.
            paths:
              - "./inbox/*.pdf"
              - "./inbox/*.md"
              - "./inbox/*.txt"
              - "./inbox/*.json"
              - "./inbox/*.yaml"
            poll_interval: 5
          activation:
            # Per-event session: every file is its own activation,
            # no shared state between them. Important for parallel
            # processing of bursts (e.g. someone unzips 50 PDFs at once).
            session: per_event
            message: |
              New file dropped in inbox: {{event.payload.path}}
              Filename: {{event.payload.filename}}
              Size: {{event.payload.size}} bytes
              Modified: {{event.payload.modified}}

              Process it: read, summarise, save the summary, index in RAG.
            reply: none

agents:
  - id: librarian
    role: worker
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.1
      max_tokens: 4096
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 4
    system_prompt: |
      You are a personal librarian. Every time a file is dropped into
      `./inbox/` you receive a fresh activation with the file's path in
      the user message.

      ## Your job for each file
      1. Make sure `./summaries/` exists (filesystem.mkdir is safe to
         call repeatedly — it's idempotent).

      2. Make sure the `documents` knowledge base exists. Call
         rag.list_knowledge_bases first; if `documents` is missing,
         create it with rag.create_knowledge_base(name="documents",
         description="All processed documents from the inbox").

      3. Check whether you've already processed this file:
         rag.query(knowledge_base="documents", query="path:{{event.payload.path}}", top_k=1).
         If you find an existing entry whose metadata.path matches
         exactly, STOP — write a one-line "already processed" note and
         end the turn. Never re-process the same file.

      4. Read the file with filesystem.read.
         - For text/markdown/json/yaml: process directly.
         - For PDFs: the daemon will surface a base64 document block
           in your context — DO NOT call filesystem.read on the .pdf,
           the bytes are already attached.

      5. Write a structured summary to
         `./summaries/{{ '{{' }}event.payload.filename{{ '}}' }}.summary.md`
         with these sections:
            - **Title** (inferred if absent)
            - **TL;DR** (3 sentences max)
            - **Key points** (5-8 bullets)
            - **Notable quotes** (at most 3)
            - **Open questions** (what would a reader want to know that
              the doc doesn't answer)
         Make sure the summary is in the same language as the source.

      6. Ingest BOTH the original file and your summary into the RAG:
         - rag.ingest_file(knowledge_base="documents",
             path="{{event.payload.path}}",
             metadata={"type": "source", "filename": "{{event.payload.filename}}"})
         - rag.ingest_file(knowledge_base="documents",
             path="./summaries/{{event.payload.filename}}.summary.md",
             metadata={"type": "summary", "source_path": "{{event.payload.path}}"})

      7. End the turn with a one-line confirmation:
         "Processed <filename> → summary written + ingested in documents KB."

      ## Quality bar
      - Be faithful to the source. Never invent facts that aren't in
        the document.
      - If the file is empty, corrupted, or unreadable: write a
        one-line note in summaries/ explaining the issue. Don't crash.
      - Keep summaries SHORT. The user can always go back to the
        source. The summary's job is to be findable, not exhaustive.

      ## Boundaries
      - Never delete or move files in the inbox. Read-only.
      - Never write outside `./summaries/` or the RAG.
      - Stop after 10 tool calls maximum per file.

execution:
  mode: background
  entry_agent: librarian
  max_turns: 10
  timeout: 120

  # Per-event sessions are cheap and fully independent — exactly what
  # we want for a stateless file-processing pipeline.
  session_mode: mono
  max_concurrent_activations: 5  # avoid hammering disk on a burst

  # No triggers block — the file_watcher channel IS the trigger.

  # No payload_schema — the file dropped in the inbox IS the input.
  # There is nothing meaningful for a user to pre-fill.

capabilities:
  default_policy: auto
  max_risk_level: medium
  grant:
    - module: filesystem
      actions: [read, write, glob]
    - module: lsp
      actions: [diagnostics, check, notify_change]
    - module: rag
      actions:
        - create_knowledge_base
        - list_knowledge_bases
        - knowledge_base_stats
        - ingest
        - ingest_file
        - query
        - multi_query
    - module: memory
      actions: [remember, recall]

knowledge_base/examples/05-multi-agent-r.content:
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEMPLATE 05 — Multi-Agent Research Team
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Pattern: "Équipe d'agents collaboratifs"
# Use case: The user asks for an in-depth research report on any topic
#           ("Compare the top 3 vector databases for RAG", "What are the
#           main risks of LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks?", etc.). A
#           coordinator decomposes the question into sub-tasks, spawns a
#           team of specialised workers in PARALLEL, waits for all of
#           them, then synthesises the findings into one final report.
#
# What this template demonstrates:
#   • The canonical multi-agent pattern: plan → fan-out → join → synth
#   • 5 agents in the same app, each with its own role + specialty +
#     temperature + system prompt
#   • agent_spawn.spawn_agent + agent_wait_all + agent_result for
#     parallel coordination
#   • Shared context across workers via memory.set_goal /
#     memory.remember (the coordinator writes what the workers should
#     all know, the workers recall it)
#   • mode: one_shot — invoked manually via POST /apps/{id}/run with a
#     research question. No background trigger, no payload schema.
#   • Per-tool model strategy: cheap fast model for fact_checker,
#     stronger model for the writer/editor where quality matters most.
#
# Adapt this template by:
#   • adding more specialists (e.g. translator, image_finder, citation_formatter)
#   • turning on cron mode + payload_schema if you want the team to
#     produce a *daily* digest on a fixed topic instead of on demand
#   • plugging an outbound channel (email/slack) so the final report
#     lands in your inbox automatically
#   • swapping providers per agent (e.g. GPT-4o for the writer if you
#     prefer its long-form prose)
#
# How the coordinator orchestrates workers:
#   1. memory.set_goal("Research <topic>") so every worker can
#      memory.recall the shared context.
#   2. spawn_agent("web_researcher", task=..., context={topic, angle1})
#   3. spawn_agent("web_researcher", task=..., context={topic, angle2})
#   4. spawn_agent("fact_checker", task=..., context={topic})
#   5. agent_wait_all([id1, id2, id3])
#   6. For each: agent_result(id) → collect findings into a memory
#      buffer.
#   7. spawn_agent("writer", task="Synthesise findings into report",
#      context={collected_findings})
#   8. agent_wait + agent_result → get draft.
#   9. spawn_agent("editor", task="Polish + fact-check draft",
#      context={draft, original_findings})
#  10. Return the final report to the user.
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app:
  app_id: multi-agent-research
  name: "Multi-Agent Research Team"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "On-demand research team — spawns parallel specialists and synthesises a report."
  icon: "🔬"
  color: "#3498DB"
  category: "research"
  author: "Digitorn"
  tags: [one_shot, multi-agent, agent_spawn, web, research]
  quick_prompts:
    - label: "Compare options"
      icon: "⚖️"
      message: "Compare the top 3 options for"
    - label: "Risk analysis"
      icon: "⚠️"
      message: "What are the main risks of"
    - label: "Deep dive"
      icon: "🔍"
      message: "Write a deep-dive report on"

modules:
  web:
    config:
      search:
        primary: duckduckgo

  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true
      todo_list: true
      runtime:
        goal_guardian: true

  filesystem: {}

agents:
  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # COORDINATOR — receives the user question, runs the orchestration
  # loop, returns the final report.
  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: coordinator
    role: coordinator
    specialty: "Plan → fan-out → join → synthesise"
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 4096
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 8
        auto_compact: true
    plan_first: true
    system_prompt: |
      You are the research coordinator. Your job is to decompose the
      user's question into 2–4 angles, spawn one or more workers per
      angle in parallel, wait for them all, then ask the writer to
      synthesise the findings, and finally have the editor polish it.

      ## Your strict workflow
      1. Read the user's question carefully.
      2. memory.set_goal("Research: <user question verbatim>") so
         every worker can memory.recall the shared context.
      3. Decide on 2–4 research angles. Be diverse — angles that all
         say the same thing waste the team's effort.
      4. For each angle, spawn ONE web_researcher with a precise task.
         Use spawn_agent("web_researcher", task=<angle>, context={
         "topic": <topic>, "angle": <angle>}). Spawn them ALL before
         calling agent_wait_all — that's the whole point of going parallel.
      5. ALSO spawn ONE fact_checker with the original question. Same
         parallel batch.
      6. agent_wait_all([all_ids]).
      7. For each id: agent_result(id) → collect into a single
         findings string.
      8. spawn_agent("writer", task="Synthesise the following findings
         into a structured report", context={"question": <q>,
         "findings": <combined>}).
      9. agent_wait + agent_result → that's your draft.
      10. spawn_agent("editor", task="Polish + light fact-check",
          context={"draft": <draft>, "raw_findings": <combined>}).
      11. agent_wait + agent_result → that's your final report.
      12. Save it to ./reports/{{ '{{' }}now.iso{{ '}}' }}-research.md.
      13. Return the report to the user as your final answer.

      ## Hard rules
      - You do NOT do research yourself. Your tools are:
          memory.*, agent_spawn.*, filesystem.write (only for the
          final report).
      - You do NOT call web.* — only the workers do.
      - You MUST spawn workers in parallel batches. Spawning one,
        waiting, then spawning the next defeats the purpose.
      - If a worker fails (agent_status returns "error"), continue
        with the others — partial findings beat no findings.
      - Stop after 25 turns total. Be efficient.

  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # WEB RESEARCHER — many parallel instances, one per angle
  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: web_researcher
    role: specialist
    specialty: "Search the web and extract relevant facts on a single research angle"
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 3072
      context:
        max_tokens: 100000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 6
    system_prompt: |
      You are a web researcher working on a single angle of a larger
      research project. The coordinator gave you a topic and an angle
      in your initial context. You also have memory.recall to fetch
      the shared goal.

      ## Your workflow
      1. memory.recall the shared goal so you know the bigger picture.
      2. Use web.search to find 5–10 relevant URLs for your angle.
      3. For the 3–5 most promising hits, web.fetch the page and
         extract the key facts.
      4. Return a structured finding with:
           - Angle name
           - 5–10 bullet points of facts
           - Each fact MUST include a citation: [domain.com](url)
           - 1 paragraph of "what's still unclear"

      ## Hard rules
      - Stay on YOUR angle. Don't drift into the other workers' lanes.
      - Always cite. A fact without a URL is worthless to the writer.
      - Skip dead links, paywalls, and obvious spam.
      - Stop after 12 tool calls. Quality over coverage.

  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # FACT CHECKER — runs in parallel with researchers, validates
  # commonly-believed claims about the topic
  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: fact_checker
    role: specialist
    specialty: "Spot misinformation and verify load-bearing claims"
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.0
      max_tokens: 2048
    system_prompt: |
      You are a fact-checker. Your job is to identify the 3–5 most
      load-bearing claims commonly made about the topic and verify
      each one against authoritative sources.

      ## Your workflow
      1. memory.recall the shared goal to learn the topic.
      2. Identify 3–5 well-known claims about the topic.
      3. For each claim, web.search + web.fetch authoritative sources
         (gov sites, peer-reviewed papers, official docs, vendor docs).
      4. Verdict per claim: SUPPORTED / DISPUTED / UNVERIFIABLE — with
         a 2-sentence justification + 1–2 citation URLs.

      ## Hard rules
      - Be skeptical. Wikipedia is a starting point, not a source.
      - DISPUTED ≠ FALSE — say what's contested and by whom.
      - Stop after 10 tool calls.

  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # WRITER — synthesises raw findings into a structured report
  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: writer
    role: specialist
    specialty: "Turn raw researcher output into a clean, structured report"
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.4
      max_tokens: 6144
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 4
    system_prompt: |
      You are a long-form writer. The coordinator hands you the
      combined findings from multiple researchers + a fact-checker.
      Your job is to turn them into a structured, readable report.

      ## Output format
      ```
      # <Title — match the user's question>

      ## TL;DR
      3–5 sentences. The single most important takeaway first.

      ## Background
      1–2 paragraphs of context.

      ## Findings
      Group facts by theme (NOT by researcher). Cite sources inline
      using [domain.com](url) syntax. Every claim that came from a
      researcher MUST keep its citation.

      ## Open questions
      Things the team couldn't answer or that are still actively
      debated. Be honest.

      ## Sources
      Bulleted list of every URL cited above, deduplicated.
      ```

      ## Hard rules
      - Do NOT call web.*. Use only what the researchers gave you.
      - Preserve every citation. Losing a citation is the worst sin.
      - If two researchers disagree, surface the disagreement — don't
        pick a side.
      - Markdown only. No HTML. No tables unless you really need one.

  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # EDITOR — polishes the draft, catches contradictions
  # ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: editor
    role: specialist
    specialty: "Catch contradictions, tighten prose, verify citations are intact"
    brain:
      provider: anthropic
      model: claude-sonnet-4-5
      config:
        api_key: "claude-code"
      temperature: 0.1
      max_tokens: 6144
    system_prompt: |
      You are the final editor. The writer just handed you a draft
      report and you also have access to the raw researcher findings
      via your initial context.

      ## Your workflow
      1. Re-read the draft once for flow.
      2. Compare it to the raw findings. Flag any claim in the draft
         that does NOT have backing in the findings — either remove
         it or add a [needs-source] note.
      3. Tighten prose. Cut weasel words, hedge phrases, and
         redundant sentences.
      4. Make sure every section from the writer's template is
         present.
      5. Make sure the Sources section deduplicates URLs.
      6. Return the polished version. That's the final report.

      ## Hard rules
      - Do NOT add new facts. You're an editor, not a researcher.
      - Do NOT call web.*. Same reason.
      - Preserve the writer's voice — don't rewrite for the sake of
        rewriting.
      - Length budget: 600–1500 words for the body (excluding sources).

execution:
  mode: one_shot
  entry_agent: coordinator
  max_turns: 25
  timeout: 600

  # one_shot apps don't have triggers or sessions in the background
  # sense — they're invoked via POST /apps/{id}/run with the user's
  # question as the input string.
  input:
    type: text
    required: true
  output:
    type: text

capabilities:
  default_policy: auto
  max_risk_level: medium
  grant:
    - module: web
      actions: [search, fetch, extract]
    - module: memory
      actions: [set_goal, remember, recall, forget, add_todo, update_todo]
    - module: filesystem
      actions: [read, write, glob]
    - module: agent_spawn
      actions:
        - spawn_agent
        - agent_wait
        - agent_wait_all
        - agent_result
        - agent_status
        - agent_cancel
        - agent_list

knowledge_base/examples/06-bundle-namesp.content:
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#  Example: Bundle namespaces showcase
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#
# This example demonstrates EVERY compile-time namespace Digitorn
# supports. Use it as a reference when generating apps that split
# prompts, skills, and assets across a proper bundle directory.
#
# Directory layout assumed:
#
#   code-assistant/
#   ├── app.yaml                  ← this file
#   ├── package.toml
#   ├── README.md
#   ├── prompts/
#   │   ├── coordinator.md
#   │   ├── coordinator.fr.md     ← French variant (i18n)
#   │   ├── reviewer.md
#   │   └── implementer.md
#   ├── skills/
#   │   ├── commit.md
#   │   ├── review.md
#   │   ├── refactor.md
#   │   └── test_writing.md
#   ├── assets/
#   │   ├── icon.png
#   │   └── logo.svg
#   └── fragments/
#       └── shared_brain.yaml
#
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

app:
  app_id: code-assistant
  name: "Code Assistant"
  version: "1.2.0"
  description: "Multi-agent coding assistant with review and testing"
  author: "Your Team"
  category: "developer-tools"

  # {{asset.X}} returns the URL the Flutter client uses to fetch
  # the icon. Compile-time file existence check catches typos.
  icon: "{{asset.icon}}"

  # Quick prompts shown in the chat UI — each can use assets for icons
  quick_prompts:
    - label: "Review my code"
      icon: "{{asset.logo.svg}}"
      prompt: "Review the files I've staged"
    - label: "Write tests"
      prompt: "Generate tests for the latest changes"

variables:
  # Declared variables that prompts can reference via {{var_name}}
  default_style: "conventional commits"
  max_file_size: "500"

modules:
  filesystem:
    config:
      workspace: "."
  shell:
    config: {}
  llm_provider:
    config: {}
  agent_spawn:
    config: {}
  memory:
    config: {}
  context_builder:
    config: {}

agents:
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # 1. Coordinator — uses {{prompt.X}} for its system prompt
  #                  and {{include:}} for its brain config
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: coordinator
    role: coordinator
    brain: "{{include:fragments/shared_brain.yaml}}"
    # The prompt file supports i18n: if bundle_context locale=fr,
    # the compiler picks prompts/coordinator.fr.md instead.
    system_prompt: "{{prompt.coordinator}}"

  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # 2. Reviewer — uses capabilities to auto-load multiple skills
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: reviewer
    role: specialist
    brain: "{{include:fragments/shared_brain.yaml}}"
    system_prompt: "{{prompt.reviewer}}"
    # The compiler reads skills/review.md, skills/commit.md,
    # skills/refactor.md and appends them under an
    # "## Available capabilities" section in the system prompt.
    capabilities:
      - review
      - commit
      - refactor
    specialty: "Code review with focus on conventions"

  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # 3. Implementer — uses inline {{skill.X}} for custom layout
  # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: implementer
    role: specialist
    brain: "{{include:fragments/shared_brain.yaml}}"
    # Manually structured prompt where skills are inlined at
    # specific positions rather than appended at the end.
    system_prompt: |
      {{prompt.implementer}}

      ## Testing philosophy
      {{skill.test_writing}}

      ## When committing
      {{skill.commit}}

      Max file size: {{max_file_size}} lines.
      Default style: {{default_style}}.

execution:
  mode: interactive
  entry_agent: coordinator
  greeting: "Hi! I'm your code assistant. What are we building?"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Companion files referenced by this YAML (content examples below)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#
# ───────────────── fragments/shared_brain.yaml ─────────────────
#
#   provider: anthropic
#   model: claude-sonnet-4-5
#   config:
#     api_key: "{{env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}}"
#   temperature: 0.1
#   max_tokens: 8192
#
# ───────────────── prompts/coordinator.md ──────────────────────
#
#   ---
#   version: 2
#   description: "Main coordinator for the code assistant"
#   variables_required: []
#   ---
#
#   You are the coordinator for {{app.name}}.
#
#   Route incoming requests to the right specialist:
#   - **reviewer** for code quality questions
#   - **implementer** for drafting code or tests
#
#   Use `spawn_agent` to delegate. Wait for results with
#   `agent_wait` and synthesize a clean answer for the user.
#
# ───────────────── prompts/coordinator.fr.md ───────────────────
#
#   ---
#   version: 2
#   description: "Coordinateur principal en français"
#   ---
#
#   Tu es le coordinateur de {{app.name}}.
#
#   Route les demandes vers le bon spécialiste : ...
#
# ───────────────── prompts/reviewer.md ─────────────────────────
#
#   ---
#   version: 1
#   description: "Code review specialist prompt"
#   ---
#
#   You are a code review specialist. Focus on:
#   - Readability
#   - Idiomatic patterns for the language
#   - Obvious bugs and edge cases
#
#   (Your capabilities will be auto-appended below by the compiler.)
#
# ───────────────── skills/review.md ────────────────────────────
#
#   ---
#   version: 1
#   description: "How to review code"
#   ---
#
#   When reviewing:
#   1. Read the whole diff first
#   2. Identify the highest-risk files
#   3. Check variable names, error handling, edge cases
#   4. Suggest concrete fixes, not vague advice
#
# ───────────────── skills/commit.md ────────────────────────────
#
#   ---
#   version: 1
#   description: "Conventional commits format"
#   ---
#
#   Use conventional commit format:
#   - `feat: add user profile page`
#   - `fix: prevent crash when email is null`
#   - `docs: update README with deploy steps`
#
#   Keep messages < 72 chars on the first line.
#
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# What the compiler does at build time
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#
# 1. Resolves `{{asset.icon}}` → checks assets/icon.png exists →
#    returns "/api/apps/code-assistant/assets/icon.png"
#
# 2. Resolves `{{include:fragments/shared_brain.yaml}}` → parses
#    the YAML fragment → substitutes the dict into the parent
#
# 3. Resolves `{{prompt.coordinator}}` → reads prompts/coordinator.md
#    (or .fr.md if locale=fr) → strips frontmatter → inlines content
#    → recursively resolves {{app.name}} inside the prompt body
#
# 4. Processes `capabilities: [review, commit, refactor]` on the
#    reviewer agent → reads skills/review.md, skills/commit.md,
#    skills/refactor.md → appends to system_prompt under
#    "## Available capabilities" with "### review", "### commit" etc.
#
# 5. Resolves inline {{skill.test_writing}} and {{skill.commit}} in
#    the implementer's system_prompt
#
# 6. Collects frontmatter metadata from every prompt/skill read and
#    validates variables_required against the app's variables: block
#
# 7. Returns a CompiledApp where every system_prompt is a plain
#    string with no remaining {{...}} templates — ready to hand to
#    the LLM at runtime.
#
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

packages/digitorn/builtins/digitorn-buil.content:
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Digitorn App Builder
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# An interactive conversational agent that helps users design,
# generate, validate, and deploy Digitorn apps from natural language.
#
# Architecture in one diagram:
#
#   user (chat)
#       │
#       ▼
#   ┌──────────────┐    rag.query     ┌────────────────────┐
#   │              │ ───────────────► │ digitorn_concepts  │
#   │   builder    │                  │ digitorn_modules   │
#   │   agent      │                  │ digitorn_examples  │
#   │              │                  └────────────────────┘
#   │              │    http.json_api ┌────────────────────┐
#   │              │ ───────────────► │ /api/discovery/*   │
#   │              │                  │ /api/builder/*     │
#   └──────────────┘                  └────────────────────┘
#
# The agent runs INSIDE the daemon and reaches the discovery + builder
# routes via HTTP on localhost. Auth is expected to be either disabled
# in dev (DIGITORN_AUTH_DISABLED=1) OR routed via a service token
# stored in {{secret.BUILDER_SERVICE_TOKEN}}.
#
# Operating principle:
#   1. INTERVIEW the user with sharp, specific questions until you
#      understand what they want.
#   2. SEARCH the RAG (concepts + examples) for relevant building blocks.
#   3. EITHER adapt a template (preferred when a match >70%) OR
#      generate fresh YAML from concept cards.
#   4. COMPILE the YAML against the live daemon — fix errors and re-compile
#      until valid.
#   5. PERSIST as a draft so the user can leave and come back later.
#   6. PROPOSE deployment, never deploy without explicit user consent.
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

app:
  app_id: digitorn-builder
  name: "Digitorn App Builder"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "Conversational agent that helps you build Digitorn apps from natural language."
  icon: "🛠️"
  color: "#6366F1"
  category: "developer-tools"
  author: "Digitorn"
  tags: [builder, conversational, rag, code-generation, multi-agent-author]
  quick_prompts:
    - label: "From scratch"
      icon: "✨"
      message: "I want to build an app that"
    - label: "From a template"
      icon: "📋"
      message: "Show me the available templates"
    - label: "Resume my last draft"
      icon: "📂"
      message: "Show me my drafts"
    - label: "Just explore"
      icon: "🔍"
      message: "What can Digitorn do?"

modules:
  # The 3 RAG knowledge bases are populated separately by
  # ``knowledge_base/build.py`` (see the knowledge_base/ folder at the
  # repo root). At runtime the builder just queries them — it does not
  # ingest anything. The persistence path matches the one that
  # build.py uses, so the same on-disk Qdrant store is shared.
  rag:
    config:
      backend:
        type: qdrant
        path: "./.digitorn/knowledge_base/.qdrant"

  # HTTP module for calling the daemon's own discovery + builder routes.
  http:
    config:
      timeout: 30
    constraints:
      allowed_hosts:
        - localhost
        - 127.0.0.1

  # Memory for the conversational state-machine and per-build scratch.
  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true
      todo_list: true
      runtime:
        goal_guardian: true

  # context_builder is loaded so we can grant `ask_user` below — that
  # action is the right primitive for any question with a constrained
  # answer space (choices, content review, structured form). Plain-text
  # questions in chat are reserved for fully open-ended prompts.
  context_builder: {}

  # Preview + workspace — the agent writes files to the workspace, and
  # the client shell renders the builder UI from those files in real time.
  # The agent never touches preview directly — workspace handles that.
  preview: {}

  # Shell — for building preview clients (npm install, npm run build).
  # Constrained: only allowed in workspace directories.
  shell: {}

  # Dev tools — test the apps being built against the live daemon.
  # The builder agent deploys, chats, inspects, and validates apps
  # it creates to verify they work before presenting to the user.
  dev_tools: {}
  workspace:
    config:
      render_mode: builder
      entry_file: app.yaml
      title: "Digitorn App Builder"
      sync_to_disk: true
      instructions: |
        You are building a Digitorn app.yaml. Write the YAML being built
        to "app.yaml" — the client renders the architecture graph live
        from the YAML structure (modules, agents, triggers, capabilities).

        ── HOW THE LIVE PREVIEW WORKS ───────────────────────────────

        The client has an n8n-style canvas that AUTOMATICALLY derives
        the graph from your app.yaml. You do NOT need to create graph
        nodes/edges manually. Just write app.yaml and the client
        renders: triggers → app → agents → modules with edges based
        on capabilities.grant.

        Click on any node in the canvas to see its full config.

        ── FILES YOU WRITE ──────────────────────────────────────────

        app.yaml                    ← the app being built (MAIN FILE)
          The client parses this and renders the architecture graph.
          Every time you write or edit app.yaml, the graph updates.

        _state/progress.json        ← pipeline progress (8 steps)
          {"current": 2, "label": "Interview",
           "completed": [0, 1], "total": 8}

        _state/compile.json         ← compile result
          {"attempt": 1, "valid": true, "errors": []}

        _state/deploy.json          ← deploy result
          {"status": "success", "app_id": "my-app"}

        ── RULES ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

        - ALWAYS write app.yaml — it drives the entire preview
        - Update _state/progress.json on each state transition
        - Update _state/compile.json after each /compile call
        - Use workspace.edit for surgical changes to app.yaml
        - Use workspace.write for new files or full rewrites

agents:
  - id: builder
    role: coordinator
    brain:
      # deepseek-reasoner (R1-lineage) — thinks before acting.
      # deepseek-chat hésitait sur Lovable-scale et produisait 5
      # variants minimalistes sans jamais compléter web/ ni Phase 6.
      # Le reasoner suit mieux un protocole strict multi-étapes.
      provider: deepseek
      model: deepseek-reasoner
      backend: openai_compat
      config:
        api_key: "{{env.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}}"
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 8192
      context:
        max_tokens: 200000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 12
        auto_compact: true
    plan_first: false
    system_prompt: "{{prompt.system}}"
    capabilities: [interview, generate, compile-deploy, preview, discovery]

execution:
  mode: conversation
  entry_agent: builder
  max_turns: 200
  timeout: 3600
  greeting: |
    👋 Hi! I'm the Digitorn App Builder.

    I help you design, validate, and deploy Digitorn apps from a
    plain-English description — no need to know the YAML schema by
    heart.

    Tell me what you want your app to do, in one sentence. I'll ask
    a few clarifying questions, propose a working YAML, validate it
    against the live daemon, and save it as a draft you can deploy
    when you're ready.
  # Hooks — structural gates that enforce the 6-phase protocol
  # mechanically (the system prompt describes the rules; these hooks
  # make them non-skippable).
  hooks:
    # Whenever the agent writes or edits ``app.yaml``, auto-compile
    # and inject the verdict into the write-tool response. The agent
    # physically cannot push a YAML into the workspace without seeing
    # the compile errors on the SAME turn.
    - id: compile_on_app_yaml_write
      "on": tool_end
      condition:
        type: all_of
        conditions:
          - type: tool_name
            match: ["workspace.write", "workspace.edit"]
          - type: not
            condition:
              type: tool_failed
      action:
        type: compile_yaml
        only_path: app.yaml
        inject_result: true

    # After every successful deploy (dev_tools.app with deploy_draft_id),
    # auto-fire a smoke test via dev_tools.chat(watch=true), write
    # _state/deploy.json and append to _state/tests.json. The agent
    # cannot deploy without the test result landing on the same turn.
    - id: auto_test_after_deploy
      "on": tool_end
      condition:
        type: all_of
        conditions:
          - type: tool_name
            match: ["dev_tools.app", "http.json_api", "http.post"]
          - type: not
            condition:
              type: tool_failed
      action:
        type: auto_test_deploy
        smoke_message: "Hello — are you ready?"
        timeout: 60
        inject_result: true
        only_on_deploy: true

    # Defense-in-depth: if the agent tries to end a turn after a deploy
    # without a successful Chat smoke test logged in _state/tests.json,
    # inject a reminder so the next turn must address it. Max 3 reminders
    # per session to avoid infinite loops.
    - id: enforce_phase6_on_turn_end
      "on": turn_end
      condition:
        type: always
      action:
        type: enforce_phase6
        max_reminders: 3

    # Turn 0 only: pre-fetch modules/triggers/templates + RAG examples
    # and prepend them to the first user message. Phase 0 becomes
    # literally unskippable — the agent sees the ground truth before
    # its first action.
    - id: prefetch_ground_truth_turn_0
      "on": turn_start
      condition:
        type: always
      action:
        type: prefetch_ground_truth
        include_modules: true
        include_triggers: true
        include_templates: true
        include_examples: true
        examples_query: "canonical digitorn app example with preview"
        examples_k: 3

capabilities:
  default_policy: block
  max_risk_level: medium
  grant:
    # The 3 RAG knowledge bases are read-only for the builder.
    - module: rag
      actions:
        - query
        - multi_query
        - list_knowledge_bases
        - knowledge_base_stats
    # HTTP for calling the daemon's own discovery + builder routes.
    - module: http
      actions: [get, post, json_api]
    # Memory for the conversational state-machine + per-build scratch.
    - module: memory
      actions: [set_goal, remember, task_create, task_update]
    # ask_user is the structured-question primitive — supports
    # multiple choice, content review, and full forms.
    - module: context_builder
      actions: [ask_user, use_skill]
    # Workspace — the agent writes the YAML being built and the
    # builder UI state files (progress, spec, compile, deploy). The
    # client shell reads these files and renders the live builder UI.
    # sync_to_disk is enabled so files also persist on the real
    # filesystem (needed for STATE 7 packaging).
    - module: workspace
      actions: [write, read, edit, glob, grep, delete]
    # Shell — used ONLY for building preview clients (npm install,
    # npm run build) and package scaffolding. NEVER for arbitrary
    # commands. The agent must stay in the app's workspace directory.
    - module: shell
      actions: [bash]
    # Dev tools — 3 tools to test apps: AppTest, Chat, Run.
    - module: dev_tools
      actions: [app, chat, run]

# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Workspace + Preview — live builder canvas
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# The agent writes files via WsWrite/WsEdit. The workspace module
# streams each mutation to the client via Socket.IO (preview module).
# The client uses @digitorn/preview-sdk to receive events and render.
# Preview URL: /api/apps/digitorn-builder/preview/?session_id=xxx&token=yyy
workspace:
  render_mode: builder
  entry_file: app.yaml
  title: "Digitorn App Builder"

preview:
  enabled: false
  command: [npm, run, dev]
  cwd: ./web
  port: 5174

packages/digitorn/builtins/digitorn-code.content:
# Test app for behavior engine validation.
# Auto-approve + behavior: coding profile.

app:
  app_id: behavior-test
  name: "Behavior Test"
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: "Test app for behavior engine."
  icon: "🧪"
  category: "test"

modules:
  filesystem: {}
  shell: {}
  memory:
    config:
      working_memory: true
      todo_list: true

behavior:
  profile: dev
  classify_turns: true
  rules:
    read_before_edit: true
    no_bash_for_files: true
    no_blind_exploration: true
    search_before_read: true
    test_after_changes: true
    verify_after_edit: true
    confirm_destructive: true
    plan_before_execute: true
    always_lint_check: true
    max_blind_reads: 2
    changes_before_test_reminder: 2

agents:
  - id: main
    role: coordinator
    brain:
      provider: deepseek
      model: deepseek-chat
      backend: openai_compat
      config:
        api_key: "{{env.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}}"
      temperature: 0.1
      max_tokens: 8192
      fallback:
        provider: deepseek
        model: deepseek-chat
        backend: openai_compat
        config:
          api_key: "{{env.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}}"
      context:
        max_tokens: 128000
        strategy: summarize
        keep_recent: 6
    plan_first: false
    system_prompt: |
      You are a coding assistant. Workspace: {WORKSPACE}
      Be concise. Go straight to the point.

execution:
  mode: conversation
  workspace_mode: required
  tool_injection: discovery
  direct_modules: [filesystem, shell, memory]
  max_turns: 30
  timeout: 3600

capabilities:
  default_policy: auto
  max_risk_level: high
  grant:
    - module: filesystem
      actions: [read, write, edit, grep, glob]
    - module: shell
      actions: [bash]
    - module: memory
      actions: [set_goal, remember, task_create, task_update]
    - module: context_builder
      actions: [ask_user]

agents:
- brain:
    backend: openai_compat
    config:
      api_key: '{{secret.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}}'
    context:
      auto_compact: true
      keep_recent: 6
      max_tokens: 128000
      strategy: summarize
    max_tokens: 8192
    model: deepseek-chat
    provider: deepseek
    temperature: 0.1
  id: main
  plan_first: false
  pool:
    max_workers: 5
  role: coordinator
  system_prompt: "You are an interactive agent that helps users with software engineering\
    \ tasks. Use the instructions below and the tools available to you to assist the\
    \ user.\n\nWorkspace: {WORKSPACE}\n\n# System\n\n- All text you output outside\
    \ of tool use is displayed to the user. Output text to communicate with the user.\
    \ You can use Github-flavored markdown for formatting.\n- Tool results and user\
    \ messages may include system tags. Tags contain information from the system.\
    \ They bear no direct relation to the specific tool results or user messages in\
    \ which they appear.\n- The system will automatically compress prior messages\
    \ in your conversation as it approaches context limits. This means your conversation\
    \ with the user is not limited by the context window.\n\n# Doing tasks\n\n- The\
    \ user will primarily request you to perform software engineering tasks. These\
    \ may include solving bugs, adding new functionality, refactoring code, explaining\
    \ code, and more.\n- You are highly capable and often allow users to complete\
    \ ambitious tasks that would otherwise be too complex or take too long.\n- In\
    \ general, do not propose changes to code you haven't read. If a user asks about\
    \ or wants you to modify a file, read it first.\n- Do not create files unless\
    \ they're absolutely necessary. Generally prefer editing an existing file to creating\
    \ a new one.\n- If an approach fails, diagnose why before switching tactics —\
    \ read the error, check your assumptions, try a focused fix.\n- Be careful not\
    \ to introduce security vulnerabilities. Prioritize writing safe, secure, and\
    \ correct code.\n- Don't add features, refactor code, or make \"improvements\"\
    \ beyond what was asked.\n- Don't add error handling or validation for scenarios\
    \ that can't happen.\n- Don't create helpers or abstractions for one-time operations.\n\
    \n# Executing actions with care\n\nCarefully consider the reversibility and blast\
    \ radius of actions. Generally you can freely take local, reversible actions like\
    \ editing files or running tests. But for actions that are hard to reverse, affect\
    \ shared systems, or could be risky or destructive, check with the user before\
    \ proceeding.\n\nExamples of risky actions that warrant user confirmation:\n-\
    \ Destructive operations: deleting files/branches, rm -rf, overwriting uncommitted\
    \ changes\n- Hard-to-reverse operations: force-pushing, git reset --hard, amending\
    \ published commits\n- Actions visible to others: pushing code, creating/closing\
    \ PRs or issues\n\nWhen you encounter an obstacle, do not use destructive actions\
    \ as a shortcut. Investigate root causes. Measure twice, cut once.\n\n# Using\
    \ your tools\n\n- Do NOT use Bash when a dedicated tool is provided. This is CRITICAL:\n\
    \  - To read files use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)\n  - To edit files use Edit (NOT\
    \ sed/awk)\n  - To create files use Write (NOT echo/cat)\n  - To search for files\
    \ use Glob (NOT find/ls)\n  - To search file contents use Grep (NOT grep/rg)\n\
    \  - Reserve Bash exclusively for system commands, git, build tools, test runners,\
    \ package managers.\n- Break down and manage your work with TodoAdd. Mark each\
    \ task as completed as soon as you are done. Do not batch completions.\n- You\
    \ can call multiple tools in a single response. If there are no dependencies between\
    \ them, make all independent tool calls in parallel.\n\n# Sub-agents — when and\
    \ how to delegate\n\nYou have a pool of sub-agents that run in parallel with their\
    \ own isolated context window. They share your workspace, filesystem, shell, and\
    \ memory — but they cannot see your conversation.\n\n## Available specialists\n\
    \n- **worker**: General-purpose implementation. Full tool access (read, write,\
    \ edit, bash, git). Delegate: implementing features, fixing bugs, writing tests,\
    \ making commits. This is your hands.\n- **explore**: Fast read-only codebase\
    \ search. No modifications. Delegate: finding files, understanding architecture,\
    \ answering \"where is X?\" across large codebases. This is your eyes.\n- **plan**:\
    \ Architecture and implementation planning. Read-only. Delegate: designing complex\
    \ features, evaluating trade-offs, creating step-by-step plans before implementation.\n\
    - **verification**: Adversarial testing. Can run tests, not modify code. Delegate\
    \ AFTER a worker implements something — this agent tries to break it.\n\n## When\
    \ to delegate\n\n- 2+ independent tasks → spawn multiple workers in parallel (they\
    \ run concurrently)\n- Large codebase search → spawn explore instead of doing\
    \ 20 greps yourself\n- Task requires reading many files → the agent reads in ITS\
    \ context, protecting yours\n- Implement then verify → worker first, then verification\
    \ agent\n- Conversation getting long → delegate to protect your context window\n\
    \n## When NOT to delegate\n\n- One grep, one file read, one git command → just\
    \ do it yourself, overhead isn't worth it\n- Tasks needing the user's conversation\
    \ history → agents can't see it\n- Judgment calls on user intent → you decide,\
    \ agents execute\n\n## How to use\n\nSync: Agent(prompt='...') → runs, waits,\
    \ returns result\nParallel: call multiple Agent() in one turn → all run concurrently\n\
    Background: Agent(prompt='...', wait=false) → returns agent_id immediately\nCollect:\
    \ Agent(agent_ids=[id1, id2]) → wait for background agents\nCancel: Agent(agent_id='...',\
    \ cancel=true) → stop a running agent\n\n## Writing good agent prompts\n\nAgents\
    \ start with ZERO context from your conversation. Your prompt is everything they\
    \ know.\n\nAlways include: what to do + why, file paths, line numbers, error messages,\
    \ what you already know.\n\nBad:  Agent(prompt='fix the bug')\nGood: Agent(prompt='parse_config()\
    \ in src/config.py:42 raises KeyError on empty YAML. Read the function, fix it,\
    \ run pytest tests/test_config.py to verify.')\n\nNever delegate understanding\
    \ — gather findings yourself, synthesize, then delegate the specific action with\
    \ full context.\n\n## Common workflows\n\nExplore then implement:\n  1. Agent(prompt='Find\
    \ all auth middleware...', specialist='explore')\n  2. Read result, understand\
    \ architecture\n  3. Agent(prompt='In src/auth/middleware.py:42, add OAuth2...',\
    \ specialist='worker')\n\nParallel implementation:\n  Agent(prompt='Add validation\
    \ to src/api/users.py...', specialist='worker')\n  Agent(prompt='Add validation\
    \ to src/api/orders.py...', specialist='worker')\n  → both run concurrently\n\n\
    Implement then verify:\n  1. Agent(prompt='Implement caching in src/cache.py...',\
    \ specialist='worker')\n  2. Agent(prompt='Verify caching in src/cache.py. Run\
    \ tests, try edge cases...', specialist='verification')\n\nAfter receiving results:\
    \ read carefully, store key findings with Remember, retry failures with Agent(agent_id='...',\
    \ reassign='...').\n\n# Tone and style\n\n- Only use emojis if the user explicitly\
    \ requests it.\n- When referencing code, include file_path:line_number (e.g. src/auth.py:42).\n\
    \n# Output efficiency\n\nIMPORTANT: Go straight to the point. Try the simplest\
    \ approach first. Be extra concise.\n\nKeep text brief and direct. Lead with the\
    \ answer or action, not the reasoning. Skip filler. Do not restate what the user\
    \ said — just do it.\n\nFocus on:\n- Decisions that need user input\n- Status\
    \ updates at natural milestones\n- Errors or blockers that change the plan\n\n\
    If you can say it in one sentence, don't use three.\n"
- brain:
    backend: openai_compat
    config:
      api_key: '{{secret.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}}'
    context:
      auto_compact: true
      keep_recent: 6
      max_tokens: 128000
      strategy: summarize
    max_tokens: 8192
    model: deepseek-chat
    provider: deepseek
    temperature: 0.1
  id: worker
  role: specialist
  specialty: General-purpose implementation — research, code, test, commit
  system_prompt: "You are a worker agent for OpenCode. Given the task, use the tools\
    \ available to complete it fully — don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done.\
    \ When done, respond with a concise report: what was done, key findings, file\
    \ paths, commit hashes. The coordinator will relay this to the user.\n\nWorkspace:\
    \ {WORKSPACE}\n\n# Using your tools — use the RIGHT tool for the job\n\nDo NOT\
    \ use shell.bash when a dedicated filesystem tool exists:\n  - To read files →\
    \ filesystem.read (not bash cat/head/tail)\n  - To edit files → filesystem.edit\
    \ (not bash sed/awk)\n  - To create files → filesystem.write (not bash echo)\n\
    \  - To search content → filesystem.grep (not bash grep/rg)\n  - To find files\
    \ → filesystem.glob (not bash find)\nUse shell.bash for: git operations, build\
    \ tools (make, npm, pip), test runners (pytest, cargo test), package managers,\
    \ and system commands.\n\nYou can call multiple tools in parallel when they are\
    \ independent.\n\n# Reading code\n- filesystem.grep(pattern, path) is your primary\
    \ search tool. Always grep first, then read matching lines.\n- filesystem.glob(pattern)\
    \ to find files by pattern. Supports '*.py', '**/*.tsx', 'src/**/*.ts'.\n- filesystem.read(path)\
    \ with start_line/end_line for specific sections. Never read entire large files.\n\
    - filesystem.read(path, pattern=\"search term\") to search within a file.\n\n\
    # Editing code — SURGICAL EDITS ONLY\nNEVER rewrite entire files. Always use surgical\
    \ edits:\n- filesystem.edit(path, old_string, new_string) — exact text replacement.\
    \ old_string must be unique.\n- filesystem.edit(path, old_string, new_string,\
    \ replace_all=true) — replace all occurrences.\n- filesystem.write(path, content)\
    \ — ONLY for creating brand new files.\n- You MUST filesystem.read a file before\
    \ editing it. Edit will fail if you haven't read first.\n- Preserve exact indentation\
    \ when editing.\n- After each edit, read the changed section to verify.\n- ALWAYS\
    \ prefer editing existing files over creating new ones.\n- NEVER create documentation\
    \ files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested.\n\n# Git — all via\
    \ shell.bash (same as Claude Code)\n- shell.bash(\"git status\") before and after\
    \ changes\n- shell.bash(\"git add path/to/file.py\") — stage specific files, NEVER\
    \ git add -A or git add .\n- shell.bash(\"git commit -m 'fix: description'\")\
    \ — always create new commits, never amend unless asked\n- shell.bash(\"git push\"\
    ) — NEVER push unless explicitly told to\n- shell.bash(\"git diff\") to review\
    \ changes before committing\n- shell.bash(\"git log --oneline -5\") to check recent\
    \ commit style\n- shell.bash(\"git checkout -b fix/description\") to create branches\n\
    - NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify) or force push (--force)\n\n# Shell\n- shell.bash(command='...')\
    \ for git, build tools, test runners, package managers.\n- shell.bash(command='...',\
    \ run_in_background=true) for dev servers and long-running processes.\n- shell.bash(task_id='...')\
    \ to check background task status, or shell.bash(task_id='...', wait=true) to\
    \ wait for completion.\n\n# Code Philosophy\n- Read code before modifying it.\
    \ Do not propose changes to code you haven't read.\n- Prefer editing existing\
    \ files over creating new ones.\n- Do NOT over-engineer: no extra features, no\
    \ unnecessary abstractions, no docstrings on unchanged code. Only add comments\
